The Quran and the Hadith

The Story of Islam

The Quran and the Hadith

The Sources of Islam

In everyday English — the book and the reports by which Islam is known

Stories by Eku

How to Read · · BEFORE WE BEGIN

Read it out loud. This story was made to be told. Read slowly, as if you were sitting among family at home — with the desert morning, the quiet of the mosque library, and the smell of old paper in the background.

The yellow boxes are the characters speaking in their own words. Change your voice a little when you read them — Zayd's slow voice, Bukhari's steady voice, Tabari's deep voice.

At the end of every part, the green box — Pause and think. Stop there. Ask questions. Let the listener speak. In this story, those questions matter as much as the story.

There are two kinds of things in this book — the Quran's verses and the evidence of history, such as old manuscripts and scholars' books; and the stories of tradition, told in the books of the Seerah and the Hadith for centuries. Where a story comes from tradition, the book says so plainly — 'the tradition tells us'. Where something rests on evidence, the book names it.

There is no picture of the Prophet Muhammad in this book — not as a man, not as a child, not as an infant, not in shadow, not from behind. That is a mark of respect for Islamic tradition, and a rule of this whole series. The pictures in this book show only manuscripts, the mosque library, the desert, light, and geometric decoration — no person at all.

This book's main story comes from the Quran, the Hadith books, al-Tabari's Tafsir, Ibn al-Nadim's Fihrist, and modern scholars. The full list of sources is at the end of the book.

Who's Who · · WHO'S WHO

Zayd ibn Thabit — a young scribe of Medina who wrote down the revelation for Muhammad; the tradition tells us that in the time of Abu Bakr and Uthman, the work of gathering the Quran was given to him.

Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Abdullah ibn Mas'ud — famous reciters (qurrā') of Medina, whose recitation people remembered.

Hafsa — daughter of Umar, wife of Muhammad; the tradition tells us the written sheets of the Quran stayed in her keeping.

Imam Bukhari (d. 870) — the most famous collector of Hadith; his book Sahih al-Bukhari is held to be the most reliable book of Hadith.

Imam Muslim (d. 875) — after Bukhari, the second great collector of Hadith; his book is Sahih Muslim.

Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah — four more collectors of Hadith; together with Bukhari and Muslim, their books are called 'the Six Books'.

Al-Tabari (d. 923) — historian and the greatest name in Tafsir; his commentary Jami' al-Bayan is still read today.

Ibn al-Nadim — a tenth-century cataloguer of books; his al-Fihrist lists all the books of his time — including books on the Quran, the Hadith, and Tafsir.

Ibn Mujahid (d. 936) — a scholar of the readings who fixed the seven famous readings (qira'at).

Modern scholars — Angelika Neuwirth (the study of the Quran), François Déroche (old manuscripts), Jonathan Brown (the history of Hadith), Harald Motzki (the testing of Hadith), Fred Donner (early Islam).

1 · What the Quran Is — Revelation, Recitation, 114 Surahs · · WHAT THE QURAN IS — REVELATION, RECITATION, 114 SURAHS

The word Quran itself means recitation — reading aloud, telling. Muslims believe the Quran is the revelation (wahy) that came down to Muhammad — the words of God, which he recited. That is why the Quran is not only read — it is recited, out loud, with melody, from memory.

The tradition tells us the revelation came down over about twenty-three years — thirteen years in Mecca, ten years in Medina. The first revelation, the tradition tells us, came in the Cave of Hira in 610 CE — and its first words were —

Surah al-'Alaq (96:1-2): Read, in the name of your Lord who created — who created the human being from a clot of blood.

The Quran has 114 surahs — long and short, all together. The longest surah is al-Baqara, with 286 verses. The shortest is al-Kawthar, with only three verses. And the count of verses in the whole book — by the Kufan count — is 6,236.

The surahs are counted in two kinds — Meccan and Medinan. The Meccan surahs, which came down in the Meccan years, are mostly short — they speak of Tawhid (the oneness of God), the Last Day, and good and evil. The Medinan surahs, which came down in the Medinan years, are mostly longer — they speak of society, law, war, and peace. By the tradition's count there are about 86 Meccan surahs and 28 Medinan surahs.

Remembering the Quran is itself an act of worship. Someone who remembers the whole Quran is called a hafiz. The tradition tells us that even in Muhammad's time, several Companions knew the whole Quran by heart — and today, all over the world, there are millions of huffaz.

Every surah of the Quran, except one, begins with the same words — 'Bismillah ar-Rahman ar-Rahim' — in the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Rahman and Rahim both mean the one who shows mercy.

Twenty-three years and 610 — the tradition's date

The twenty-three years of revelation (thirteen in Mecca, ten in Medina) and the year of the first revelation, 610 CE, are the tradition's dates, from Ibn Ishaq's Seerah and the Hadith books. There is no contemporary document for them — these dates come from tradition.

6,236 verses — a way of counting

The count of the Quran's verses, 6,236, is the Kufan count, the one most widely used today. Other counts give a slightly different number — such as 6,214 or 6,226 — because some counts treat the Basmala as a verse and others do not. The words of the book are the same — the way of counting differs.

Meccan and Medinan — the tradition's division

The division into Meccan and Medinan surahs is the tradition's division. Some surahs contain both Meccan and Medinan verses, and scholars disagree about some surahs, whether they are Meccan or Medinan. This book gives the tradition's count (86 Meccan, 28 Medinan) — the division is not certain.

Pause and think — Quran means recitation — reading aloud. Why would a book not be only for reading — why must it also be recited?

2 · How the Quran Was Collected — Abu Bakr, Hafsa's Sheets, Uthman's Mushaf · · HOW THE QURAN WAS COLLECTED — ABU BAKR, HAFSA'S SHEETS, UTHMAN'S MUSHAF

In Muhammad's time the Quran was both written down and remembered. The tradition tells us that as soon as a revelation came, the scribes of the revelation (kuttab al-wahy) wrote it down — on palm leaves, on bones, on leather, on slabs of stone. The most famous of these scribes was Zayd ibn Thabit. And at the same time, many Companions remembered the Quran — it was in their hearts.

The tradition tells us that after Muhammad's death, in the Battle of Yamama (632), many of the huffaz were killed. Umar was afraid — if the huffaz kept dying, the Quran would be lost. He told Abu Bakr — gather the Quran in one place. Abu Bakr called Zayd ibn Thabit and said — gather the Quran.

The tradition tells us Zayd gathered the Quran — from the written sheets and from the memory of the huffaz. For every verse he asked for two proofs — one written, one remembered. In this way the sheets of the Quran — the suhuf — were prepared. These sheets stayed first with Abu Bakr, then with Umar, and then with Hafsa — Umar's daughter, Muhammad's wife, in whose house the sheets were kept.

The tradition tells us that in Uthman's time, when Islam had spread far and wide, quarrels began in the distant cities over the Quran — one city read it one way, another city another way. Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman warned Uthman — before people start fighting, fix one standard text of the Quran.

The tradition tells us Uthman called Zayd ibn Thabit and three more scribes of the Quraysh — and from Hafsa's sheets they made standard copies of the Quran — the mushaf. These copies were sent to the great cities — Mecca, Medina, Kufa, Basra, Damascus. And the tradition tells us Uthman ordered that the other copies be burned — so that only one text would remain.

The first mushaf looked different from the mushaf of today. It had no dots and no vowel marks. Without dots, many Arabic letters looked alike — 'b', 't', 'th' — all the same. It was only the rasm — the skeleton of the letters, without dots. The reader knew from memory which letter was which. The dots and vowel marks were added later — the tradition says the work on dots began with Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali.

The story of the gathering — a story of tradition

The story of the Quran's gathering in Abu Bakr's time — after Yamama, on Umar's advice, Zayd ibn Thabit's work, the rule of two proofs — comes from Sahih al-Bukhari. No contemporary document of this event survives — the story is tradition's.

Uthman's mushaf — the date is tradition's

The story of the standard copies made in Uthman's time — Hudhayfa's warning, the copies made from Hafsa's sheets, their sending to the cities, the burning of other copies — comes from Sahih al-Bukhari. Its year, by tradition about 650 CE (25 AH), is tradition's date — the manuscript evidence cannot confirm the year.

Hafsa's sheets — a matter of tradition

The keeping of the Quran's sheets with Hafsa comes from Sahih al-Bukhari — a matter of tradition.

Rasm, dots, and vowel marks — what the evidence says

That the early mushafs had no dots or vowel marks is shown by the old manuscripts themselves too — see the Sana'a and Birmingham manuscripts in Part 9. Linking the dots to Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali is a matter of tradition — scholars disagree about when and how the dots were added.

Pause and think — The Quran was first remembered, then written — and then the writing was checked against the memory. Memory and writing — which is more trustworthy? And why?

3 · The Readings — The Seven Readings and Different Ways of Reading · · THE READINGS — THE QIRA'AT, THE SEVEN READINGS

From the very beginning, the Quran was read in different ways. The tribes of Arabia spoke different dialects — one said 'a', another said 'e'. The tradition tells us the Quran came down in seven ahruf (seven ways) — so that every tribe could read it in its own dialect. This is in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim.

With time, many ways of reading spread — and scholars had to decide which ways were sound. Ibn Mujahid (d. 936) fixed seven famous readings — the seven qira'at. Later scholars added three more — and today ten readings are recognised.

How do the readings differ? Most differences are small — a dot, a vowel, the pronunciation of a word. But sometimes the word itself differs. The most famous example is the fourth verse of Surah al-Fatiha — in the reading of Hafs it is read 'Māliki yawm al-din' (Master of the Day of Judgement), and in the reading of Warsh it is read 'Maliki yawm al-din' (King of the Day of Judgement). The meaning is almost the same — but the word is different.

Today most Muslims in the world read the reading of Hafs from 'Asim — that is the reading in which the printed mushafs are found. In North and West Africa the reading of Warsh from Nafi' is read. Both readings are accepted in tradition — neither is held to be wrong.

Seven ahruf — a matter of Hadith

'The Quran came down in seven ahruf' — this Hadith is in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim. But what exactly 'seven ahruf' means — seven dialects, seven ways, or something else — scholars have debated for centuries. This book does not decide what it means exactly — the Hadith is told, and the debate is recorded in its own note.

Seven readings — the tradition's count, and different ways of reading

The count of seven readings is the one fixed by Ibn Mujahid — it is the tradition's count. And the different ways of reading — such as Hafs and Warsh — are recorded in the tradition itself, not a new discovery. This book states both things plainly — the count of seven is tradition's, and the different readings truly exist.

Pause and think — One book, read in seven ways — and all of them held to be right. Must a book have only one right way of reading — or can several ways be right?

4 · What the Hadith Are — Isnad, the Chain, and the Six Books · · WHAT THE HADITH ARE — ISNAD, THE CHAIN, THE COLLECTIONS

After the Quran, the second great source of Islam is the Hadith. Hadith means report, news. Every Hadith tells what Muhammad said, what he did, or what he approved.

Every Hadith has two parts — the isnad and the matn. The matn is the words of the Hadith — what was said. The isnad is the chain — who heard it from whom. Like this — 'A heard it from B, B heard it from C, C heard it from Aisha, that Muhammad said…' — that chain is the isnad. No Hadith is accepted without its isnad — that is why it is said — 'The isnad is part of the religion.'

The great work of collecting the Hadith happened in the ninth century — about two hundred years after Muhammad's death. The most famous collector was Imam Bukhari (d. 870). The tradition tells us he examined six hundred thousand reports, and kept about 7,275 of them in his book Sahih al-Bukhari — counting repeated Hadith.

After him came Imam Muslim (d. 875) — his book Sahih Muslim has about 7,500 Hadith, counting repeated ones. These two books are called the Sahihayn — the Two Sahihs.

With these two there are four more books — the Sunan of Abu Dawud, the Sunan (Jami') of al-Tirmidhi, the Sunan of al-Nasa'i, and the Sunan of Ibn Majah. These six books together are called al-Kutub al-Sitta, the Six Books.

There were books of Hadith before these too — the oldest famous book is al-Muwatta of Imam Malik (d. 795) — which records, along with Hadith, the practice (amal) of Medina. And the Musnad of Ahmad ibn Hanbal is famous too.

Bukhari's count — the tradition's count

The story that Bukhari examined six hundred thousand reports and kept 7,275 is the tradition's count — it is written in later books. Modern scholars point out that these counts include repeated Hadith and different chains — the same Hadith came through many chains, so the count grew large.

'The Six Books' — a later grouping

The grouping of 'the Six Books' (al-Kutub al-Sitta) was made by later scholars — Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud, Tirmidhi, Nasa'i, and Ibn Majah did not themselves put their books in this group. The group was fixed around the eleventh century.

Pause and think — Every Hadith also tells who heard it from whom — the whole chain. Before believing something, is it necessary to know who it was heard from?

5 · How Scholars Grade Hadith — Sahih, Hasan, Da'if · · HOW SCHOLARS GRADE HADITH — SAHIH, HASAN, DA'IF

There are hundreds of thousands of Hadith in the books — but are they all sound? That is the question the muhaddithun (the scholars of Hadith) asked — and they made a way of testing Hadith.

The test looked at five things. First — is the chain unbroken, every link joined? Second — are the narrators honest? Third — is their memory firm? Fourth — is there any hidden flaw ('illa) in the Hadith? Fifth — does the Hadith clash with any stronger Hadith?

After this test, a Hadith was given a grade. Sahih — sound, strong — the chain firm, the narrators trustworthy, no flaw. Hasan — fair, good, but a little weaker than sahih — the narrator's memory a little less firm. Da'if — weak — the chain broken, or a narrator not trustworthy. And mawdu' — fabricated — made up by someone on purpose.

In practice, the grade meant this — from a sahih Hadith, law and belief are taken. A hasan Hadith is also taken — but with a little caution. From a da'if Hadith no law is taken — it is sometimes told to encourage good deeds, but only while saying that it is weak. A mawdu' Hadith is thrown away — it must not even be told, except to say that it is fabricated.

Schacht's doubt — one modern view

Joseph Schacht (1950, 'The Origins of Muhammadan Jurisprudence') said that most Hadith are not from Muhammad's time — they were made up in the eighth and ninth centuries and then attributed to Muhammad. His argument was that the chains of Hadith grew longer with time — the later the book, the longer the chain. This is one view, not a verdict — the next note gives the other view.

Motzki's defence — a second modern view

Harald Motzki and other scholars challenged Schacht's view. With isnad-cum-matn analysis (testing the chain and the words together) they showed that many Hadith go back to the first Islamic century — their chains and their words both point to the same old source. This book does not decide which view is right — both views are recorded in their own notes, and the debate continues today.

Pause and think — One scholar calls the same Hadith sahih, another calls it da'if. Can truth have grades — or is truth only truth?

6 · The Sunnah — The Prophet's Example in Daily Life · · THE SUNNAH — THE PROPHET'S EXAMPLE IN DAILY LIFE

Sunnah means way, path. In Islam, the Sunnah means Muhammad's way, his example. How he prayed, how he ate, how he met people, how he treated his neighbours — all of this is the Sunnah.

The Quran says — Surah al-Ahzab (33:21): 'In the Messenger of God you have an excellent example.' That is why Muslims look at the Sunnah along with the Quran — the Quran gives the command, and the Sunnah shows what that command looks like in life.

The Hadith books are full of the small things of daily life. The tradition tells us Muhammad ate with his right hand, and said 'Bismillah' before eating. He greeted people with salam — 'As-salamu alaykum' — peace be upon you. He visited the sick, looked after his neighbours, and was honest in trade.

There is a difference between Hadith and Sunnah — the Hadith is the report in which something is recorded, and the Sunnah is the practice that comes from the report. A Hadith may say that Muhammad did such-and-such — and the way that comes from it is the Sunnah. Scholars look at both together.

33:21 — the Quran's own words

'In the Messenger of God you have an excellent example' is in Surah al-Ahzab (33:21), the Quran's own words.

The small things of daily life — from Hadith

Eating with the right hand, greeting with salam, visiting the sick, and honesty in trade come from the Hadith books — especially Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim. These Hadith have different grades — some sahih, some hasan — which is why this book tells them with 'the tradition tells us'.

Pause and think — The Quran says — pray. The Sunnah shows — how to pray. Is it enough to know the command — or is it also necessary to know how the command is carried out?

7 · Tafsir — The Commentators, from al-Tabari to Ibn Kathir · · TAFSIR — THE COMMENTATORS, FROM AL-TABARI ONWARDS

The verses of the Quran are sometimes short — and people would ask — what does this mean? The work of answering that question is Tafsir, the commentary on the Quran.

The first Tafsir was made from the words of the Companions — what they had heard from Muhammad, they told. Then came the words of the Tabi'un (the generation after the Companions). And then the great books of Tafsir began to be written.

The greatest Tafsir was written by al-Tabari (d. 923) — Jami' al-Bayan. Tabari gathered for every verse all that had been said before — the words of the Companions, the words of the Tabi'un, and the words of the scholars of his time — each with its chain. His Tafsir is in thirty volumes — and it is still read today.

After Tabari came other great commentators. Al-Zamakhshari (d. 1144) stressed language — the meaning of every Arabic word. Fakhr al-Din al-Razi (d. 1210) stressed reason — he raised questions on every verse and answered them. Al-Qurtubi (d. 1273) stressed law — what command comes from every verse. And Ibn Kathir (d. 1373) stressed Hadith — he explained every verse from Hadith.

The ways of Tafsir are different — one explains a verse from another verse, one from Hadith, one from the words of the Companions, one from language, one from reason. And the commentators also disagree with one another — and their disagreement is recorded in the books. Tafsir does not mean there is only one right answer — Tafsir means the search for the answer goes on.

Tafsir is still being written today — great commentaries were written in the twentieth century too, and scholars are still writing on the Quran today. Every age's commentator reads the Quran with the questions of his own age.

Tabari and the later commentators — dates and books

Al-Tabari died in 923 CE, and his Tafsir Jami' al-Bayan is in thirty volumes — this comes from Ibn al-Nadim's al-Fihrist and modern scholars. The dates and books of Zamakhshari, Razi, Qurtubi, and Ibn Kathir come from the same sources.

Pause and think — Five commentators say five things about one verse. Does that mean none of them is right — or does it mean there are five things in the verse?

8 · What the Quran Teaches — Tawhid, Justice, Mercy, the Human Being · · WHAT THE QURAN TEACHES — TAWHID, JUSTICE, MERCY, THE HUMAN BEING

The first and greatest teaching of the Quran is Tawhid, the oneness of God. One whole surah, Surah al-Ikhlas (112), is only about this —

Surah al-Ikhlas (112:1-4): Say — He is God, the One. God, the Self-Sufficient. He did not give birth to anyone, and He was not born. And there is none equal to Him.

The second great teaching is justice. The Quran says — Surah al-Nahl (16:90): 'God commands justice and kindness.' And in Surah al-Nisa (4:135) it is said — 'Stand firm for justice — even if it is against yourselves, or against your parents and relatives.'

The third great teaching is mercy. Every surah, except one, begins with the same words — God is Rahman, Rahim. And the Quran says — Surah al-Anbiya (21:107): 'We sent you only as a mercy — for all the worlds.'

And the fourth great teaching is the human being. The Quran says — Surah al-Isra (17:70): 'We have honoured the children of Adam.' And in Surah al-Hujurat (49:13) it is said — 'We made you into peoples and tribes — so that you may know one another.'

These four things — Tawhid, justice, mercy, and the honour of the human being — are the heart of the Quran's teaching. Everything else — prayer, fasting, charity, pilgrimage — stands around these four things.

The verses — the Quran's own words

All the verses in this part — Surah al-Ikhlas (112:1-4), Surah al-Nahl (16:90), Surah al-Nisa (4:135), Surah al-Anbiya (21:107), Surah al-Isra (17:70), Surah al-Hujurat (49:13) — are the Quran's own words. Their meaning in English is given in this book's own simple English — it is not an official translation.

Pause and think — Tawhid, justice, mercy, the honour of the human being — four things. If you had to choose only one, which would you choose — and why?

9 · The Manuscripts — Sana'a, Topkapi, and Birmingham · · THE MANUSCRIPTS — SANA'A, TOPKAPI, AND BIRMINGHAM

Where are the oldest manuscripts of the Quran? In the libraries of mosques, in the treasuries of palaces — and sometimes, hidden away in attics, found by chance.

The Sana'a manuscripts — in 1972, the roof of the Great Mosque of Sana'a, the capital of Yemen, was being repaired. Workers found a pile of old papers in a room above the ceiling — fragments of Quran manuscripts, centuries old. Some of these parchment pages are from the seventh and eighth centuries — the first century of Islam.

Some of the Sana'a pages are palimpsests — old writing washed off, and new writing written over it. The writing underneath — the undertext — differs a little from today's standard text. The order of some words is different, some words are different. Scholars have read these pages — and found that the differences are small — of words, of order — but the book is the same.

The Sana'a manuscripts — what they show and what they do not show

The Sana'a manuscripts were found in 1972 in the Great Mosque of Sana'a — this comes from the work of François Déroche and other scholars. They show early manuscripts, and different ways of reading — as tradition itself records. They do not show that there was a different Quran, or that the book was made up later. No fragment clashes with the standard text in any major way. They show that the first Muslims wrote the book with small differences — as tradition itself says.

The Topkapi manuscript — in the Topkapi Palace in Istanbul there is a very old manuscript of the Quran. The tradition says it is Uthman's own copy — the very copy he had made. But scholars, looking at its script, say it may be from the eighth century or later — not from Uthman's time.

The Birmingham manuscript — in 2015 came the news that two pages of the Quran kept in the library of Birmingham, England, had been radiocarbon tested — and their parchment dated to between 568 and 645 CE. These pages are among the oldest Quran manuscripts in the world — and their words match today's standard text.

The Topkapi manuscript — tradition against scholars

That the Topkapi manuscript is Uthman's copy is tradition's story — the palace's own account. Scholars, such as François Déroche, looking at its script, say it is from the eighth century or later. This book does not decide which is right — the tradition's story is told, and the scholars' view is recorded in its own note.

Radiocarbon testing — what it tests

The radiocarbon test of the Birmingham pages — 2015, Oxford University — gave the date of their parchment: 568-645 CE. Radiocarbon testing dates the parchment (the animal skin) — not the ink. The writing could be later than the parchment — but scholars hold that the writing is early too, because the pages' words match the standard text.

Pause and think — The old pages show what the book first looked like — without dots, without vowel marks. Does a book stay the same book if its writing changes?

Closing Reflection · · CLOSING REFLECTION

In this book we have seen two things — the Quran, which was recited and remembered; and the Hadith, which was heard and tested. One book that came down over twenty-three years, and thousands of reports that were gathered over two hundred years.

And we have seen how both were looked after — the scribes wrote, the huffaz remembered, Uthman fixed one text, Bukhari tested, Tabari explained, and today's scholars are reading the old pages and testing them.

In the next part we will hear the story of the people who built a society with this book and these reports — the Four Caliphs, and the question that arose the moment Muhammad left — who now? But first, take one question with you —

The Quran was recited, the Hadith were heard — both first went in through the ear, and only then came onto paper. When something is written down, does it stay the same — or does something change?

Pause and think — What touched you most in this book — the memory of the huffaz, Uthman's mushaf, Bukhari's testing, Tabari's Tafsir, or the old pages of Sana'a? And why?

Sources · · SOURCES

The Quran — Surah al-Fatiha (1:4), Surah al-Baqara (2), Surah al-Nisa (4:135), Surah al-'Alaq (96:1-2), Surah al-Ikhlas (112:1-4), Surah al-Nahl (16:90), Surah al-Anbiya (21:107), Surah al-Isra (17:70), Surah al-Hujurat (49:13), Surah al-Ahzab (33:21).

Sahih al-Bukhari — the book of Hadith; the story of the Quran's gathering (Abu Bakr, Zayd, Hafsa, Uthman), the Hadith of the seven ahruf, and the Hadith of daily life are taken from it.

Sahih Muslim — the book of Hadith; the Hadith of the seven ahruf and the Hadith of daily life are taken from it too.

The Sunan of Abu Dawud — the book of Hadith; one of the Six Books.

The Sunan (Jami') of al-Tirmidhi — the book of Hadith; one of the Six Books.

Al-Tabari's Tafsir (Jami' al-Bayan) — the greatest book of Tafsir; what is said here about Tabari and Tafsir is taken from it and from Ibn al-Nadim.

Ibn al-Nadim's al-Fihrist — a tenth-century catalogue of books; on Tabari's Tafsir and the books of that time.

Ibn Mujahid's Kitab al-Sab'a fil-Qira'at — on the seven readings; on the count of the readings and the difference between Hafs and Warsh.

Angelika Neuwirth, The Qur'an and Late Antiquity — on the study of the Quran.

François Déroche, The Qur'an and its Manuscripts — on the old manuscripts, Sana'a and Topkapi.

Jonathan Brown, Hadith: Muhammad's Legacy in the Medieval and Modern World — on the history, collection, and testing of Hadith.

Harald Motzki, The Origins of Islamic Jurisprudence — on the testing of Hadith and isnad-cum-matn analysis.

Joseph Schacht, The Origins of Muhammadan Jurisprudence (1950) — on the sceptical view of Hadith.

Fred Donner, Muhammad and the Believers — on early Islam and the early community of the Quran.

Wherever this book says 'the tradition tells us', the matter is taken from the books of the Seerah and the Hadith — not from the evidence of history. Where a matter rests on evidence, its name is given in its own note.
